articles.title: Ethiopian armed groups forge alliance against government
articles.summary: Former adversaries say they will settle differences as fears grow of expanding war in Ethiopia.
articles.body:
Seven Ethiopian armed groups have formed an alliance aimed at overthrowing the government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.

The groups announced the alliance on Sunday, saying that they would work together to set up an inclusive transitional government.

“We have established a joint alliance called the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, known in short as the Alliance for Survival,” the groups said in a joint statement .

The alliance includes the Amhara Fano National Movement, a coalition of Fano factions that has fought federal forces in the Amhara region since 2023; the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Abiy took office; and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), which has fought federal forces in Oromia since 2018.

Four smaller groups – the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF), the Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front (Ugugumo), the Benishangul Peoples’ Liberation Movement and the Gumuz Peoples’ Democratic Movement – make up the rest.

The groups’ leaders had been talking to form the alliance for about a year, a source close to Fano told Al Jazeera on Sunday.

The announcement comes weeks after clashes in the northern region of Tigray, one of the most serious breaches yet of a 2022 peace deal, deepened fears of a return to full-scale war.

Fighting has gripped parts of Oromia since 2018 and Amhara since 2023.

Abiy came to power in 2018 promising sweeping reforms. He freed journalists, activists and other political prisoners and revoked bans on many political parties after taking power.

But his opponents and human rights activists accuse his government of reversing those gains in recent years.

In the statement, the alliance accuses the government of imposing “dictatorial rule” that has pushed the country towards break-up.

It also says a transitional government guided by a charter would work to end the wars, protect rights and open a national dialogue.

Jaal Marroo, the OLA’s military leader, told a local broadcaster earlier this month that they had met several times before settling on the final announcement.

Zemene Kassie, the Fano leader, first publicly indicated that deals had been reached in an interview with the Swiss newspaper Le Temps, published on August 16.

The government has not publicly commented on Sunday’s announcement.

Fano fought alongside federal forces against Tigray’s fighters in the Tigray war of 2020 to 2022, which killed hundreds of thousands.

Amhara and Tigray also both claim Western Tigray, which Amhara nationalists have administered since the war ended.

Ethiopian academic Eyob Tilahun told Al Jazeera on Sunday that the competing groups had agreed to have a dialogue and form an alliance “in the best interests of the public”.

“Those allied forces believe that they all face a survival threat from the government,” Eyob said.

The 2022 peace agreement, signed in Pretoria, South Africa, ended the war between the federal government and Tigray’s forces but left disputes over disarmament and the TPLF’s legal status unresolved.

In mid-July, the TPLF declared the 2022 Pretoria peace deal “effectively dead”.

articles.title: Patrick Clancy in his own words: Top takeaways from grieving father's first interview
articles.summary: Patrick Clancy told "60 Minutes" that baby Callan died in his arms after four agonizing days and recalled apologizing to his son in their final moments.
articles.body: Patrick Clancy begged for just one of his children to survive, held baby Callan as he died in his arms and revealed why he forgave Lindsay after she killed their three children. Speaking with correspondent Ross Douthat on CBS News' "60 Minutes," the grieving father shared new details about his children's final moments, what Lindsay told him about the killings and the online attacks he says are hurting their legacy. The interview aired after Lindsay's triple-murder trial ended in a mistrial. Her attorneys argued she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and was not criminally responsible, while prosecutors maintained she knew what she was doing. From his desperate plea at the hospital to the online claims that followed the mistrial, Patrick described how the tragedy has shaped every part of his life. PATRICK CLANCY SPEAKS OUT AFTER HUNG JURY IN LINDSAY CLANCY CASE, ADDRESSES PROSPECT OF ANOTHER TRIAL ‘Just give me one’ Patrick said he clung to hope that Callan might survive after his siblings, 5-year-old Cora and 3-year-old Dawson, were found dead inside the family's Duxbury, Massachusetts, home. Doctors had restored the baby's heartbeat, and Patrick told Douthat he began imagining the life he could still give his youngest child. "I remember that night, I really thought there was a chance that Callan would live," Patrick said. "And I remember just thinking, ‘Just give me one. Just give me one kid,’" he continued. "And I would raise him as best I could, and I would give him the best life I possibly could. And I'd tell him about his brother and sister." Patrick said that hope faded when he reached Boston Children's Hospital and saw the look on a doctor's face. Callan's heart continued beating for four days. Patrick became emotional as he recalled apologizing to his son and spending his final moments beside him. "I said, ‘I'm so sorry,’" he told Douthat, his voice breaking. "And I got to hold him. I got to lay down next to him. And he died in my arms." While Callan remained in the hospital, Patrick said he held his son's hand and used his free hand to write about all three children. He told Douthat he feared their memories might fade if he did not put them into words. Lindsay never asked for forgiveness The tributes Patrick wrote also included words of forgiveness for Lindsay. He said she has never asked him to forgive her, but he chose to give that forgiveness anyway. LINDSAY CLANCY DESCRIBED A MALE VOICE ORDERING HER TO ‘KILL HER CHILDREN AND KILL HERSELF’: TESTIMONY "I saw headlines that said, you know, ‘killer mom’ and ‘baby murderer,’ ‘monster,’ and none of them were accurate," Patrick said during the interview. "I believe that it was her mental illness that caused that." Patrick said he also feared anger would consume him if he could not forgive her. "I felt that if I didn't get there, I would be eaten up inside," he said. When Patrick asked Lindsay whether she remembered killing their children, he said she described the memory as dreamlike. LINDSAY CLANCY'S FAMILY WAS 'VERY CONCERNED' ABOUT HER MENTAL HEALTH IN THE MONTHS BEFORE SHE KILLED HER KIDS "She said it was like a dream, and she remembered it much in the way you would remember a dream after waking up," he told Douthat. Patrick said he did the best he could as Lindsay's condition worsened but must live with what happened. "I think I did the best I could with what I had at the time, and I live with the outcome," he said. "I live with it every day." Grief left him unsure he would survive Patrick told Douthat his grief became so overwhelming that he questioned whether he would live to see another birthday. "There was a time where I didn't think I would live to see my 35th birthday, and I was completely fine with it," he said. Patrick later left Duxbury for New York City, where he could grieve without being recognized. Five weeks after the move, on what would have been Callan's first birthday, he went to St. Patrick's Cathedral, lit a candle and told his son, "I love you, buddy." "And I walk out on Fifth Avenue and I start crying my eyes out, and nobody cared," Patrick recalled. For Patrick, being able to cry without drawing attention was exactly what he needed. "I thought, this is where I need to be," he said. "I can grieve." His Manhattan apartment remains filled with reminders of the children, including a baby sloth Cora carried everywhere and a photograph of Callan wearing an oversized bow tie, "60 Minutes" showed. Patrick said they also return to him in vivid dreams. In one, Cora walked into the kitchen of the family's former home and hugged him. "I just looked at her and it was like I basically just said, ‘Where have you been?’" he recalled. "Those dreams are so real." ‘Trial by TikTok’ fueled painful attacks The mistrial unleashed what Douthat described as a "trial by TikTok," with online sleuths and influencers spreading baseless theories portraying Patrick as uncaring, unfaithful and even responsible for the children's deaths. "It's deeply harmful to the legacy of my children," Patrick said. "It is a huge distraction from what really matters here, which is perinatal mental health, and it's done real harm to real people." LINDSAY CLANCY’S EX-HUSBAND DETAILS ‘BIG SPIRAL’ AS EXPERT SAYS ONE PART ‘SCARED ME’ IN MOM’S MURDER TRIAL He said the repeated accusations have made it painful to be in public and warned that people may start believing false claims if they see them often enough. "After seeing lie after lie after lie, they start to believe it," Patrick said. "And that's what we're left with." Patrick said he sought answers from Postpartum Support International, psychiatrists and other experts. Those conversations helped him begin processing what happened. A new marriage and keeping his children’s memory alive Patrick's wife, Dr. Rachel Danis, joined him for the "60 Minutes" interview and recalled first learning about his children after noticing their photograph on his phone during a coffee outing. "I just asked, ‘Who are those cuties?’" Danis told Douthat. "And Pat had said, ‘Those are my kids.’" When she asked whether they lived in Massachusetts, Patrick told her they had died. Patrick and Danis met through a New York running club in January 2024. Their relationship deepened as they continued running together, and they married in New York City this April. The couple also discussed starting a family. Asked what he would tell a future child about Cora, Dawson and Callan, Patrick said all of his children would remain part of the same family. "You have different relationships with your kids, but they're all your kids," he said. "And I can't wait to tell them about their brothers and sister." Prosecutors have not announced whether they will try her again.

articles.title: The Sahel and the UN: a smaller footprint, a different role
articles.summary: As UNGA 81 begins, the UN faces a changing Sahel demanding greater sovereignty.
articles.body:
For a decade, the United Nations’s most visible role in the Sahel was its peacekeeping mission in Mali.

The United Nations Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission in Mali (MINUSMA) was established by the Security Council in 2013. Its mandate was terminated in June 2023 at the request of Mali’s transitional government, and the mission completed its withdrawal by the end of that year.

But the end of MINUSMA did not end the UN’s engagement with the region.

Its political work continues through the UN Office for West Africa and the Sahel (UNOWAS), while the wider UN system remains involved in humanitarian and development work.

What has changed is the space in which that engagement takes place.

Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger formally left the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) on January 29, 2025. The three countries have also deepened cooperation through the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), putting sovereignty and strategic autonomy at the centre of their political message.

The humanitarian pressures, meanwhile, have not eased.

Displacement, insecurity, food insecurity and other pressures continue to cross borders, even as governments increasingly insist on handling their security and political affairs on their own terms.

The question is what influence the UN can exercise after the departure of the peacekeeping force that once represented its most substantial presence in the region.

What does the UN’s presence look like now?

The UN’s role today is less about troops and more about diplomacy, mediation, humanitarian assistance and development.

UNOWAS is a special political mission rather than a peacekeeping operation. Its work includes preventive diplomacy, good offices, political mediation, conflict prevention and support for political dialogue.

“The influence the UN can actually exercise is narrow. The AES states have stripped away the mechanisms that once gave outside institutions leverage, leaving ECOWAS and the Rome Statute, and building their own confederation and joint force instead,” said Mubarak Aliyu, a political and security analyst in Nigeria.

In February 2026, the Security Council extended UNOWAS’s mandate until January 31, 2029, while requesting an independent strategic review of its mandate and activities, to be finalised by September 30, 2026.

The review comes as West Africa’s political landscape is being reshaped by military governments, new regional alliances and a stronger emphasis on sovereignty.

Russia has also become an important part of that changing security picture.

“What has actually shaped events this year is Russia’s Africa Corps, which helped Mali’s and Niger’s military governments survive shocks the UN was never positioned to influence, functioning mainly as regime protection rather than counterinsurgency,” Aliyu said.

“Moscow’s leverage extends into the Security Council chamber too, since its veto shapes what collective action the Council can attempt on Mali in the first place.”

Kabir Adamu, founder and managing director of Beacon Security and Innovations Limited, an Abuja-based firm that provides security solutions in Nigeria, the Lake Chad Basin and the Sahel, said the UN should shift its approach away from large deployments of UN troops to diplomatic and towards diplomatic and development solutions.

“Looking ahead, the UN’s priorities in the Sahel should promote effective security sector governance and security sector reform. This will mean pivoting from traditional, large-scale peacekeeping to deep-rooted and core preventive strategies and diplomacy that addresses the root causes of fragility, conflict and violence, as well as instability,” Adamu said.

For the United Nations, diplomacy has become more important as governments turn to other security partnerships and regional arrangements.

How has sovereignty changed the political space?

Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have made sovereignty and strategic autonomy central to their political outlook and built the AES as a framework for closer cooperation.

Their departure from ECOWAS has changed the regional architecture through which West African governments have traditionally dealt with political and security crises.

The UN still works with regional organisations, including ECOWAS and the African Union, but governments no longer share one political framework or the same approach to external engagement.

Consequently, for the UN, maintaining vital political channels has become potentially more difficult.

Adamu said the fragmented security architecture means the UN should seek to work with and through regional organisations and groups, rather than establishing its own large-scale forces.

“As national security structures remain weak and extractive, and regional security architecture fragments, marked by the rise of the Alliance of Sahel States and shifting ECOWAS dynamics, the UN should prioritise pragmatic, inclusive mediation to bridge divides between Sahelian and coastal states, while actively bolstering alternative, functioning frameworks like MNJTF [Multinational Joint Task] and the Accra Initiative,” he said.

Have the problems in the Sahel gone away?

The retreat of peacekeepers has not removed the pressures that brought international organisations into the region in the first place.

Displacement, armed violence, organised crime, food insecurity and climate pressures continue to overlap across the Sahel.

Climate change is perhaps not the root cause of the instability, but environmental and economic pressures can add to existing vulnerabilities, particularly where state institutions are weak and communities are already dealing with conflict and displacement.

For the UN, humanitarian work remains one of the areas where engagement can continue, even when governments reject large-scale military intervention.

Humanitarian work also places greater emphasis on local and regional capacity.

“Crucially, the UN must double down on the core UNISS pillars of governance, resilience, and security by integrating climate-peace initiatives and empowering local capacities, ensuring that international engagement remains flexible, locally owned, and focused on sustainable, multidimensional stability rather than solely militarised responses,” Adamu said.

While the UN cannot determine the security partnerships of sovereign governments or force political processes on authorities that reject them, it can still facilitate dialogue, support humanitarian operations and raise regional crises before the wider international community.

The 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly opened on September 8, 2026, with its General Debate due to begin on September 22.

The UNGA meets with no UN peacekeeping mission in Mali and with Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger outside ECOWAS, while the AES has become a separate framework for their political and security cooperation.

“That leaves the UN closer to an advocate and service provider than a shaper of outcomes,” Aliyu said. “It can report, brief, fund aid operations and press for access, but it cannot compel it or offer the regime security that has made Russia indispensable to the military governments.”

Yet for the Sahel, insecurity, displacement, humanitarian needs and economic and climate pressures remain.

In the changed regional environment, the UN’s influence is more likely to come through diplomacy than force, through access rather than authority, and through regional relationships rather than a large international security presence.

articles.title: Missing Carnival Panorama passenger jumped overboard off Mexico's coast
articles.summary: A male passenger jumped overboard from the Carnival Panorama as it sailed from Puerto Vallarta back to Long Beach, triggering a major search.
articles.body: A passenger traveling on a Carnival Panorama cruise jumped overboard as the ship was wrapping up the last full day of a week-long sailing. The cruise departed Long Beach, California, on September 13 and was headed back there from Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, when a male passenger jumped overboard, according to the cruise line. "Carnival Cruise Line confirmed Saturday that a male guest aboard Carnival Panorama jumped overboard while the ship was sailing from Puerto Vallarta, Mexico to Long Beach, California," a Carnival Cruise Line spokesperson told Fox News Digital. CRUISE PASSENGER HAILED AS HERO AFTER JUMPING INTO WATER TO SAVE 84-YEAR-OLD MAN "When notified of a missing guest, the ship's team initiated search and investigation procedures, including reviewing CCTV footage and notifying both the U.S. and Mexico Coast Guards," the statement continued. The spokesperson said the company is providing support to the family who was traveling with the guest. "Our thoughts and prayers are with them and their loved ones," the statement reads. CARNIVAL CRUISE PASSENGER, 67, FOUND DEAD WHILE SNORKELING OFF THE COAST OF AUSTRALIA DURING EXCURSION According to a Reddit user who said they were aboard the sailing, announcements regarding a missing guest were heard at around 11 a.m. on Saturday. Carnival Panorama had departed from its last port of call on the sail, Puerto Vallarta, at 8 p.m. on Thursday. The call for the missing guest was repeated several times over the next several hours. At about 3 p.m., the ship reportedly turned around. Another announcement was made at about 3:30 p.m. that there would be a shipwide search, and all guests were told to return to their staterooms. Security visited each of the staterooms to scan guests' ship identification cards, which is a standard procedure in the event of a search. An hour later, another announcement suggested the search was continuing, and guests were instructed to remain in their staterooms. At around 5 p.m., the captain and cruise director said the guest had been confirmed overboard after a review of onboard cameras, adding that local authorities would continue the search and rescue operation and guests were no longer required to stay in their staterooms. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The family and traveling companions of the missing guest were notified of his disappearance and were offered support from the care team. Shortly after 7 p.m., guests were told that the ship was expected to reach Long Beach at 9 a.m. Fox News' Jessica Mekles contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump administration readies sweeping sanctions against ICC, reports say
articles.summary: Measures targeting the court itself could disrupt payments, IT services and investigations.
articles.body:
The Trump administration is reportedly preparing sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) that could disrupt the tribunal’s finances and day-to-day operations.

The US sanctions would prohibit most transactions with the ICC after a grace period of six to seven months, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday.

The move would mark a sharp escalation in Washington’s campaign against the Hague-based court by targeting the institution itself rather than individual judges and prosecutors.

The Trump administration plans to announce the sanctions soon, according to the Reuters news agency, quoting two sources familiar with the matter.

The Journal, citing anonymous officials, said a decision could be finalised during this week’s United Nations General Assembly gathering in New York or soon afterwards.

If imposed, the measures would generally bar US citizens and companies from providing the ICC with money, goods or services without a licence from the US Treasury.

Banks and other companies often take an especially cautious approach to US sanctions because they rely on access to the American financial system.

The ICC president and registrar have previously warned that sanctions on the organisation as a whole could interfere with its ability to buy information technology and insurance services, hire investigators and make routine payments, including salaries for American employees.

The ICC was created in 2002 to prosecute individuals accused of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity when national authorities are unable or unwilling to do so.

Washington has already sanctioned more than a dozen ICC judges and prosecutors under an executive order signed by President Donald Trump in February 2025.

In August, it added the court’s President Tomoko Akane and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye to the list, with restrictions on them taking effect on September 17.

The United States has never joined the court.

The Trump administration says the court has exceeded its authority by pursuing officials from countries that are not ICC members.

Relations deteriorated sharply after the court issued arrest warrants in November 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

Israel, like the US, is not an ICC member and rejects the court’s jurisdiction.

Washington has also objected to an earlier ICC investigation into alleged abuses in Afghanistan involving US personnel.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced a campaign in July to further isolate the court and urged other countries to withdraw from it.

Trump’s move adds to growing opposition to the ICC in recent months.

Chad and Venezuela moved in July to withdraw from the court, following Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger.

Four US-based rights groups sued the Trump administration in August, arguing that existing sanctions obstruct their legal and human rights work.

articles.title: Powerful explosions at Syrian army site near Aleppo injure at least four
articles.summary: Officials urge civilians to stay away from the site in al-Eis near Aleppo after a series of explosions.
articles.body:
Powerful explosions at a weapons depot in northern Syria have injured at least four people, according to state media, with officials urging the public to stay away from the site.

The explosions occurred early on Monday at a Syrian army site in the vicinity of the town of al-Eis, south of the city of Aleppo, the state-run SANA news agency reported.

The cause of the explosions was not immediately clear.

Faisal Mohammad Ali, the head of civil defence operations in Aleppo, told SANA that rescuers have evacuated four injured people from the site.

Al Jazeera’s Obaida Hitto, reporting from Aleppo, said a series of blasts has followed the initial explosion.

“The explosions are audible from a few kilometres away from the site. We have now seen a series of ambulances and fire trucks enter towards the position,” he reported.

Aleppo Governor Azzam al-Gharib urged residents not to leave their homes for the time being, adding that “hospitals, ambulance and emergency teams are on full alert”.

Roads leading to the site of the explosions were closed “to ensure the safety of civilians”, Aleppo’s Internal Security Command said.

A resident of Aleppo’s Hamdaniyeh neighbourhood told the AFP news agency that they heard a “huge explosion” and when they went up to the roof could see “large flames in the distance”.

Several such blasts have previously occurred in Syria, which is emerging from more than a decade of civil war following the toppling of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in late 2024.

An explosion of unknown origin killed 11 people at a military site in the eastern province of Deir Az Zor on Friday.

Earlier this month, an explosion at a weapons depot belonging to the Ministry of Defence killed 14 people and injured 11 in Syria’s northwest Idlib province.

Five people were killed just over a week earlier in the same area when a vehicle carrying munitions exploded.

articles.title: Patrick Clancy talks about grief, forgiveness and the future with ‘60 Minutes’ after Lindsay Clancy mistrial
articles.summary: In his first interview since his ex-wife’s trial, Patrick Clancy opened up about his grief at losing his three children and said that he tried his best before the tragic killings in Massachusetts.
articles.body: In his first interview since his ex-wife’s trial, Patrick Clancy opened up about his grief at losing his three children and said that he tried his best before the tragic killings in Massachusetts. “I think I did the best I could with what I had at the time,” he said in an interview with CBS’ “60 Minutes” that aired Sunday. “And I live with the outcome. I live with it every day.” Lindsay Clancy, 36, sought treatment for depression and was hospitalized before she killed their three children Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, in January 2023. Her high-profile murder trial, which ended with the jury split 11-1 and a mistrial declared on Sept. 4, centered on a defense that argued she was not criminally responsible in their deaths because she was suffering with postpartum psychosis. Patrick Clancy said he did not know much about postpartum illness before. “I could piece together what it was like to be really, really anxious or depressed. But I didn’t know how to manage a postpartum illness,” he said. “I think mental illness has this ability to be tragically deceptive,” he said. “So I’m sure there are things that I didn’t see.” Clancy had testified during the trial. He took the stand for two days, recounting the horrors of the evening of Jan. 24. He described running errands at his then-wife’s behest, only to return home to find her with cuts to her neck and wrists after throwing herself out their bedroom window in a suicide attempt. In the basement, he found his children with exercise bands around their necks. Patrick Clancy, who has since remarried, said on “60 Minutes” that he asked Lindsay Clancy if she remembered what happened. “She said it was like a dream. And she remembered it much in the way you would remember after waking up,” he said. He said the news headlines depicting “killer mom,” and “monster” were not accurate. “I believe that it was her mental illness that caused that,” he said. After finding his children in the basement, he hoped Callan might survive. The infant had been airlifted to a Boston hospital after the two others were found dead, and Patrick Clancy said he was told doctors were able to re-establish a heartbeat. “That night, I really thought there was a chance that Callan would live,” he said. “And I remember just thinking: Just give me one. Just give me one kid,” Clancy said. “And I would raise him as best I could. I would give him the best life I possibly could. I’d tell him about his brother and sister. And I was holding out hope for that.” “And then when I got to the hospital, I saw the doctor and I saw the look on her face, and I knew it wasn’t going to be a good prognosis,” he said. Clancy spent four days with his injured son at the hospital, time for which he said he grateful. He said he was able to lay next to his child and hold him, and his son died in his arms. The highly-watched trial spawned a maelstrom of conspiracy theories, some going as far as accusing Patrick Clancy of committing the murders. “It’s deeply harmful to the legacy of my children,” Clancy said in the “60 Minutes” interview. “It is a huge distraction from what really matters here, which is perinatal mental health, and it’s done real harm to real people.” Lindsay Clancy’s defense attorney Kevin Reddington also rejected those conspiracy theories, telling NBC News, “it’s readily apparent that Patrick has been set upon and his life has been turned upside down into a nightmare that he doesn’t deserve. Period. Full stop.” Patrick Clancy’s lawyer also slammed “so-called influencers and outright conspiracy theorists” who have published “what they know to be outright falsehoods that Patrick was somehow involved in the death of his young children and other vile claims.” The attorney said “every appropriate measure will be pursued to hold them accountable, including legally.” Patrick Clancy said that the online rumors and comments and conspiracy theories were hurtful. “It’s painful to see, and it makes it difficult to be in public,” he said in the interview. “And it’s possible that some of those people, after seeing lie after lie after lie, they start to believe it. And that’s what we’re left with.” What happened in the trial During his testimony, Patrick Clancy described how wife’s mental state deteriorated despite meeting with psychiatrists, and changing medications and doctors. He said he had never seen Lindsay harm their children before. He testified that earlier on the day of the killings, Lindsay appeared to be “having one of her best days.” She had taken her daughter Cora to a doctor’s appointment, and later built a snowman with the children. Lindsay Clancy’s defense didn’t deny that she killed her children. Her attorney argued she was not criminally responsible in their deaths because she was suffering with postpartum psychosis, a rare condition that can alter a new mother’s sense of reality and is considered a psychiatric emergency. Clancy claimed she heard a voice commanding her to kill her children, according to testimony at trial. The prosecution had argued she was not suffering from psychosis and was deliberate in planning the killings and in sending her then-husband out on errands while she killed her children. After the killings, Patrick Clancy had publicly issued a statement of support for his then-wife, saying she was kind and loving, and wishing for her to find peace. Asked on “60 Minutes” whether Lindsay Clancy had ever asked for forgiveness, Patrick Clancy said, “No. But I gave it to her.” A move to Manhattan, for anonymity and grieving After the tragedy in Duxbury, a town of just 16,000 where he and his family lived, Patrick Clancy moved to New York City to seek a degree of anonymity. On what would have been Callan’s first birthday, he went into St. Patrick’s Cathedral in Manhattan, lit a candle “and I said, ‘I love you, buddy.’” “And I walk out on Fifth Avenue, and I start crying my eyes out,” he said. “And nobody cared.” “I thought, ‘this is where I need to be. I can grieve,’” he said. He met Dr. Rachel Danis in a running club and the two got married in April and are starting a family, they said on the program. “I always try to take some of the weight from Pat,” Danis said on the news show. “I know I can’t fix — I can’t bring his kids back, but if I can honor them and allow Pat to grieve but also just continue to honor them in the present, I guess that’s all I can do.” Clancy said he plans to tell his new family about the children that he lost. “I think every parent can agree: You have different relationships with your kids, but they’re all your kids,” he said. “And I can’t wait to tell them about their brothers and sister.” If you or someone you know is struggling or in emotional distress, call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org 24/7, to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For additional resources, visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources.

articles.body: The United States has issued a fresh advisory against travel to Iran, urging American citizens to avoid the country “for any reason” and calling on those already there to leave immediately amid heightened tensions and the threat of further escalation in West Asia.In a security alert, the US Virtual Embassy in Iran said the regional security situation remained complex and cautioned that travellers could face flight cancellations, airspace closures and other disruptions.“Do not travel to Iran for any reason. US citizens should leave Iran now,” the advisory said.The US Mission urged Americans in the region to remain highly vigilant and closely monitor developments affecting airports, airlines and border crossings.It also warned that procedures at Iran’s land borders could change without notice and advised travellers to check the entry requirements of any country they may seek to enter.The US also cited the activities of Iranian-backed Houthi forces, which have carried out attacks in Saudi Arabia, including strikes targeting civilian airports.“Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports. This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly,” the alert said.The United States further warned that its diplomatic facilities, including locations outside the Middle East, have been targeted in the past and that Iran or groups supportive of Tehran could target US interests, businesses and institutions overseas.American citizens were advised to enrol in the Department of State’s Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) to receive security updates and facilitate contact with US diplomatic authorities during emergencies.The alert also urged citizens to avoid demonstrations, large gatherings and areas with a heavy police presence, while maintaining a low profile at locations publicly associated with the United States.In the event of an aerial attack, Americans were instructed to stay away from windows and glass doors, avoid fallen debris and monitor official communications.The alert comes amid an escalating confrontation between the United States and Iran, with Washington maintaining military and maritime pressure on Tehran and Iranian officials warning of retaliation against US interests in the region.The latest warning follows a separate US security alert for Americans and US government personnel in Saudi Arabia. articles.title: Cindy Crawford’s son, model Presley Gerber, dies at 27
articles.summary: The son of Cindy Crawford, Presley Gerber, has died at the age of 27, her representative confirmed to CNN.
articles.body: The son of Cindy Crawford, model Presley Gerber, has died at the age of 27, her representative confirmed to CNN. The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner’s office said Gerber died Sunday while at a rehab facility. The cause of death was not listed. Crawford’s publicist confirmed the news, telling CNN: “The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time.” Born in California in 1999, Gerber was one of two children Crawford shared with businessman Rande Gerber. Like his sister, Kaia Gerber, he entered the modeling industry at a young age, making his runway debut for Italian label Moschino aged just 16. He went on to walk for brands including Burberry, Dolce & Gabbana, Bottega Veneta, as well as US labels Tommy Hilfiger and Ralph Lauren. Gerber modeled in campaigns for Calvin Klein, Celine, Pepsi and Omega, and for magazines including GQ Style and The New York Times Style Magazine. He also worked as an investor and entrepreneur, according to a biography on DNA Model Management, which signed Gerber in 2019. DNA Model Management — which also represents his sister, as well as fashion figures like Emily Ratajkowski and Adwoa Aboah — did not immediately respond to CNN’s request for comment. Gerber had been open about his mental health struggles and drug use in recent years. Appearing on the Studio 22 podcast in 2023, he discussed using his platforms to raise mental health awareness, calling the issue “such a big part of my life.” He ran his own “Mental Health Mondays” initiative and worked with NGOs including the LA homelessness charity, A Sense of Home, according to DNA Model Management. Last December, Gerber posted a video to Instagram detailing his use of prescription medication, including antidepressants and Xanax for panic attacks. “Unfortunately, I’ve had a lot of loss in many different forms recently,” he said in the since-removed video. “So that is not an excuse, but it’s the reason why I am where I’m at now.” Commenting on the video at the time, Crawford had written “Presley — we love you and you are not alone.” More recently, the 60-year-old supermodel posted to Facebook to mark her son’s 27th birthday in July, writing: “I’m so proud of the man you’ve become, but I’ll always see you as my little boy!” Earlier this month, Kaia spoke about her brother’s struggles with addiction in American Vogue’s September issue cover story. “When something like that happens in a family, it kind of levels everyone,” she said. “I think that’s also why I started to self-identify as the easy one and never wanted to ask for help.” She went on to praise his role within the family. “My parents for most of our lives were very, very private and didn’t share anything — and now we have this absolute teacher, my brother, who says, ‘I’m gonna be very human for everyone,’” she is quoted as saying. This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title: Converse apologizes and pulls sneaker ad that critics said included racist imagery
articles.summary: The sneaker company Converse has removed a social media ad that sparked outrage among critics who viewed it as evoking the Ku Klux Klan and lynching.
articles.body: The sneaker company Converse has removed a social media ad that sparked outrage among critics who viewed it as evoking the Ku Klux Klan and lynching. The Instagram ad photo showed K-pop singer Karina wearing a skirt and holding a pair of Chuck 70 X sneakers. Critics lashed out online, saying that a white triangular image created by lighting on the skirt resembled a KKK hood and that the way she held the sneakers made them look like the dangling feet of a lynching victim. Converse, owned by Nike, issued a statement apologizing and saying it removed the ad. “We’re sorry,” said the statement, first released on Friday. “We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognize that we got this wrong. We removed it from our channels and are working to remove it everywhere it appeared. This should not have happened and we will do better.” Converse, based in Boston, declined on Sunday to answer questions seeking additional information, including how the company screens ads before they are posted and how the ad was approved. Karina and her management company, SM Entertainment Group, did not immediately respond to messages through their Instagram accounts. Retailers and top fashion brands have issued a string of apologies over the years for products criticized as being racially insensitive. Last month, retailer Target pulled a children’s Halloween costume from its shelves after widespread social media backlash, apologizing for selling a garment that critics said evoked racist minstrel caricatures. The Converse photo sparked swift criticism, including calls for staff involved in the ad to be fired and for a boycott of the company. In a slew of comments on social media, posters questioned how the ad could have cleared the company’s advertising vetting process. Other commenters defended Converse, saying they didn’t believe it was intentional. Lee Merritt, a civil rights attorney based in Texas, posted on Instagram that Converse’s apology “doesn’t undo what got past legal, marketing and leadership at every step.” Converse, founded in Malden, Massachusetts, in 1908, makes the iconic Chuck Taylor All Star sneaker. It was first released in 1917 as a non-skid basketball shoe, adding the signature of Taylor — a basketball player who promoted the sneaker — in 1934, according to the company’s website.

articles.title: The tragic death of a woman who testified against her mafia father after he murdered her mother
articles.summary: It was a necklace that helped Denise Cosco identify her mother after she was murdered by her father and boyfriend.
articles.body: It was a necklace that helped Denise Cosco identify her mother after she was murdered by her father and boyfriend. Cosco, her father Carlo, and mother Lea Garofalo went on holiday together in November 2009 on what she thought was a chance for them to reconcile after Lea testified to authorities about her husband’s drug dealing for the Calabria ’Ndrangheta crime syndicate. But Carlo was in no mood to forgive. It would be another three years before Lea’s body was discovered. “When they showed me the necklace among the remains of her charred bones, I knew immediately that it was hers and that she had given her life to save me,” Cosco later said. “I can never thank her for that.” Like her mother, Cosco spent years hiding out under Italy’s witness protection program as a result of testifying against the mob. Both left the program frustrated with the Italian state. And their connections did not end there. Most tragically of all, Lea was 35 when she died – the same age as Denise when she fell to her death from the apartment she shared with her husband and four-year-old son in Rome earlier this month. Prosecutors are now trying to determine if the mafia was behind her death by “inciting” her apparent suicide. She left no note to explain her mindset. The case has prompted renewed debate in Italy over the safety of those who enter the state witness program for mafia syndicates and the physical and psychological burden that weighs on anyone who dares to challenge the mafia’s code of silence. ‘You gave me strength’ Cosco spent six years living under an assumed identity created for her by the Italian state after testifying against her father and her then-boyfriend, Carmine Venturino, over the kidnapping, torture, dismemberment and murder of her mother in November 2009. Both were sentenced to life in prison, although Venturino’s term was later reduced. Lea Garofalo’s murder was deemed a revenge attack after she testified against her husband, her brother and others about their alleged criminal drug dealing in Milan. Her testimony, motivated by her desire to protect her daughter from growing up in a mafia family, made her one of Italy’s most celebrated “turncoats,” or state’s witnesses collaborating with authorities against organized crime. Since her murder, streets, parks and schools have been named after her in recognition of her courage. Garofalo’s remains were found after Venturino admitted to involvement in both her murder and the concealment and burning of the body, eventually pointing authorities to the hiding place. At her mother’s funeral in October 2013, Cosco, then 22, spoke from behind bulletproof glass and thanked her mother. “This is a very difficult day for me, but you gave me strength,” she said of her mother. “I will never stop thanking you.” Garofalo and Cosco were among a scant few women who have chosen – or been able – to escape their crime families, albeit with inarguably detrimental results. Around 6,000 people are enlisted in Italy’s witness protection program, according to Italy’s Interior Ministry, but many face difficulty in staying protected. Anti-mafia prosecutor Alessandra Cerreti, who has persuaded dozens of women to testify against crime families across all Italy’s crime syndicates, admits the risks are high. Under Italian law, investigators have 180 days to work with the potential collaborators to determine if they are telling the truth or are instead actually still faithful to their crime families. “We have a short period of time to understand the entire situation,” Cerreti told CNN, adding that there are often budget restrictions and a lack of corroborators, especially right after someone escapes the crime family. If they are accepted into the program, protection is evaluated every four years to see if the turncoat is still cooperative, or if they have returned to the mafia family or simply disappeared. The collaborators are given a place to live, a false identity, a job and a life story that can be corroborated if anyone checks, but they live on very little money and rarely feel safe, Cerreti said. Garofalo, who hid her daughter in convents and tiny towns around Italy until she left witness protection in 2009 – the year she was murdered – cited her reasons for departure as “financial hardship” and “the constant threat of being removed from protection” because the state was unable to corroborate any of the claims in her testimony due to the lack of other witnesses Under Italian law, if a turncoat’s testimony cannot be corroborated, or if a threat is no longer perceived, the state removes protection. “If we had more time, we could better protect those who do come forward, which would make it easier for others to do the same,” Cerreti said. “But it often feels as risky to flee as it does to stay.” ‘The mafia kills in many ways’ Cosco’s husband was home at the time she fell from the window and had been questioned but is not a suspect. It is unclear if he even knew she was under witness protection. She was only referred to as Denise Cosco by authorities after she died on September 10, having spent four days in the hospital. Her father, speaking through his lawyer from prison, said the two had started to reconcile, Italian media reported, but no details of what that meant have yet emerged. A criminal investigation has been opened and Cosco’s phones and electronic devices have been sequestered to determine if she had been facing threats from anyone tied to the murder of her mother, or if the pressure, guilt and sadness of her complicated life had become too much. Her lawyer, Enza Rando, who helped her testify against her father and boyfriend in 2009, told CNN the state was also to blame for not providing enough protection and support for those who cross crime gangs. “The mafia kills in many ways. It kills by creating true monsters in the lives of those left behind,” Rando said. “ Cosco’s death has shaken anti-mafia investigators. Naples public prosecutor Nicola Gratteri, who has led hundreds of state informants away from their criminal families to collaborate with the courts, told reporters her death was a setback for the fight against organized crime and could make it even more challenging to get people to testify. It has also rattled those who live under protection. Giuseppe Carini, who lives under an assumed identity as a witness in the murder of a Catholic priest who preached against the Sicilian Cosa Nostra in 1993, wrote in an open letter shared by his lawyer that Cosco had been let down by the “highest levels of the State and the government.” “It has been said that witnesses of justice are courageous people, that Lea and Denise were courageous women and as such will never die, but we do not want gravestones or epitaphs carved in marble. Witnesses of justice have the sacrosanct right to live and to live a normal life,” he said. After Cosco died, her aunt Marisa Garofalo posted a photo of her holding up a T-shirt bearing her late mother’s name. Since she was living under a false identity when she died, only her trusted family members even knew what Cosco looked like. “Now I can show you your beautiful eyes,” her aunt wrote. “No one will be able to decide for you anymore, you will no longer have to hide.”

articles.title: Pakistan airstrikes on Afghanistan: 3 killed, several injured as conflict fears grow
articles.summary: South Asia News: At least three people were killed and several others injured in a Pakistani airstrike targeting Afghanistan's northeastern Kunar province, Tolo News r.
articles.body: At least three people were killed and several others injured in a Pakistani airstrike targeting Afghanistan's northeastern Kunar province, Tolo News reported on Monday, citing a provincial official.The military strike is supposedly in retaliation for suicide bombing at a police station compound in northwestern Pakistan, raising fears that tensions between the neighbouring nations could once again turn into open fighting.Pakistan and Afghanistan were involved in their most serious military confrontation in years in February. The latest escalation comes days after the Taliban warned that it would defend Afghan territory against any Pakistani military action.Taliban warns of 'crushing response'Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid, ahead of the imminent Pakistani strikes, had warned Islamabad against carrying out strikes inside Afghanistan, saying Kabul would respond militarily if its territory is attacked.In an interview with Al Arabiya English, Mujahid rejected Pakistan's allegations that militant groups based in Afghanistan recruit, train and launch attacks against Pakistan.“If Pakistan invokes Article 51 to violate the sanctity of Afghan territory, Afghanistan has the right to defend its country, and we will do so,” Mujahid said.He said any Pakistani military operation inside Afghanistan would amount to a violation of Afghan sovereignty and could trigger a strong response from Kabul.Mujahid was responding to comments by a Pakistani military spokesperson, who had told Al Arabiya English that militant groups were using Afghan territory to recruit, train and arm fighters before sending them into Pakistan.Kabul denies sheltering TTPMujahid rejected those allegations and said the Taliban administration does not allow the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, to operate from Afghan soil.He also denied that the Taliban government supports armed groups carrying out attacks against other countries. Instead, Mujahid said Pakistan should examine its own internal security problems, arguing that violence involving the TTP and Baloch armed groups existed before the Taliban returned to power in 2021.Pakistan has repeatedly accused militant groups of operating from Afghanistan and has pressed Kabul to take action against them. The Taliban has consistently denied allowing Afghan territory to be used for attacks against Pakistan.Afghanistan keeps door open for talksDespite his warning of military retaliation, Mujahid said Kabul was still willing to engage with Islamabad through dialogue.He called for stronger intelligence-sharing arrangements and greater bilateral cooperation to address security concerns along the two countries' border.Mujahid also backed a possible mediation role for Saudi Arabia, saying Riyadh has good relations with both Afghanistan and Pakistan and could help the two sides resolve their differences.Relations between Kabul and Islamabad have remained strained over militant activity along their shared border. The latest airstrike, coming amid fresh security concerns, risks further worsening those ties and could lead to another confrontation between the neighbours.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Manhunt underway in California after armed suspect allegedly points gun at people, shoots at officers
articles.summary: California deputies urge local residents to lock their doors amid a manhunt for a suspect wanted for several felonies, including pointing a firearm at people.
articles.body: Deputies in California are searching for a man believed to be armed and dangerous after allegedly murdering a woman and shooting at others, according to authorities. Derek Spencer, 44, is wanted for several felonies, including pointing a firearm at people in Placer County on Sunday, according to the Placer County Sheriff's Office. Authorities said Spencer was initially wanted after allegedly pointing a firearm at people earlier Sunday. During the search for Spencer earlier on Sunday, deputies found him in the Iowa Hill area. Spencer rammed a patrol vehicle before fleeing the area, triggering the manhunt. DRAMATIC VIDEO SHOWS SWAT VEHICLE RAMMING TRACTOR DURING TENSE OREGON STANDOFF Spencer also fired shots at law enforcement officers and helicopters assisting law enforcement. No law enforcement officers were injured during the search for Spencer. Everyone in the Iowa Hill area is urged to lock their doors and remain inside. In an update on Sunday night, the sheriff's office said the search remained ongoing, noting the search is very challenging due to the area being very large, with dense forest and steep, rugged terrain. SUSPECT IN DEATHS OF 5 FOUND DEAD AFTER COPS UNCOVER GRIM SCENE AT RURAL PROPERTY OUTSIDE PORTLAND But during the search, deputies located a murder victim they believe was killed by Spencer. "As tactical teams worked to clear a home where Spencer had been earlier in the search, they located an adult female who had been shot and killed inside the home. At this point in the investigation, it’s believed Spencer murdered the woman before fleeing into the surrounding forest," deputies said. The sheriff's office is being assisted by multiple other law enforcement agencies. articles.title: Man and police officer wounded in gunfire near Ontario synagogue on Yom Kippur
articles.summary: TORONTO — A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire Sunday near a synagogue in Ontario as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said.
articles.body: TORONTO — A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire Sunday near a synagogue in Ontario as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said. The man was hospitalized in life-threatening condition. The province’s Special Investigations Unit said the exchange of gunfire happened near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, about 110 miles east of Toronto. Belleville police said the officer encountered the man around 7:10 p.m. and that both were taken to a hospital. Police have not said what led to the shooting or whether the synagogue or Jewish community was targeted. They said there was no risk to public safety and asked people to avoid the area while officers investigated. The Special Investigations Unit, the civilian agency that investigates serious incidents involving police, said it sent investigators to the scene. Belleville police said they would not provide further information while the investigation was underway. Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the shooting took place outside the synagogue as people gathered for Yom Kippur. “I’m disgusted by the shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville earlier this evening as Jewish community members gathered to mark Yom Kippur,” Ford said in a post on social media. Ford said Jewish people “have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear” and called for those responsible to be arrested and prosecuted. “My thoughts are also with the police officer who was shot, along with their family and loved ones,” Ford said. York Regional Police said there was no known threat in the region but residents should expect increased patrols at places of worship. Sunday’s shooting comes months after Prime Minister Mark Carney warned that Canada was failing its Jewish community amid a surge in antisemitism. Carney cited shootings at Jewish schools, firebombings of synagogues and attacks on community centers and Jewish-owned businesses. His government announced millions in additional funding to help faith-based institutions pay for security infrastructure, training and personnel. Synagogues in the Toronto area have also previously been targeted by gunfire. In March, shots damaged the entrances of synagogues in Vaughan and Toronto. No one was injured. Police later arrested three suspects in connection with those shootings.

articles.title: U.S. proposes exchanging AI safety alerts with China, Bessent says
articles.summary: The United States has proposed a new AI safety notification mechanism for President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to consider at their summit in Washington this week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday.
articles.body: HONG KONG — The United States has proposed a new AI safety notification mechanism for President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to consider at their summit in Washington this week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday, amid global concern over whether the world’s two leading AI powers can work together to contain the technology’s potential dangers. Speaking to reporters after daylong talks in New York with Chinese officials, Bessent said the two sides had discussed setting up a new U.S.-China AI dialogue that would include a mechanism for alerting each other to AI-related incidents that could affect national security. “We think that just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important,” he said, adding that the two sides had agreed to meet again on the AI issue. AI is expected to be high on the agenda when Trump and Xi meet Thursday, especially after warnings from AI leaders in the U.S. that the technology could pose an existential threat within a few years. Trump has dismissed such concerns as a “hoax” while agreeing with AI executives such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei that the U.S. must not allow China to pull ahead in the global AI race. Experts caution that the Trump-Xi summit is unlikely to produce any major agreement on AI, citing the high level of distrust between the two countries. China has interpreted calls to slow down AI development as targeted at its own progress. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told reporters that AI talks would not affect U.S. export controls on advanced chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment that have hindered Chinese AI companies. Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng and China’s chief trade negotiator, Li Chenggang, did not comment to reporters as they left the talks at JPMorganChase headquarters. A Chinese readout of the talks published by Xinhua, China’s state-run news agency, did not mention the U.S. proposal and said only that the two sides had discussed AI. Xinhua said the two sides also had “frank, in-depth and constructive exchanges on important economic and trade issues of common concern, including implementing the consensus reached in previous trade consultations and promoting bilateral trade and investment.” A major question ahead of this week’s summit is whether Trump and Xi will agree to extend a fragile trade truce that is set to expire Nov. 10. Bessent and Greer said the two sides had agreed to operationalize a new “Board of Trade” that was announced during Trump’s visit to Beijing in May, and were exploring the potential for lower tariffs on “non-sensitive” products. On the Chinese side, Greer said, those could include consumer goods and low-tech items, while U.S. exports of energy, agricultural goods and medical devices are also being considered. He did not say whether that meant tariffs on those items would be lowered now or that they would only be exempted from fresh duties in the future. “There is a world where you have a relatively small subset of American and Chinese goods that can be traded in a balanced way that are non-sensitive,” he said. “Then in the future, as trade actions come up, we can consider them as a class unto themselves.”

articles.title: New Zealand man to honour father and renowned Suffolk artist
articles.summary: He has created a book of Peter Partington's work, and proceeds will go towards a bursary for wildlife artists.
articles.body:
The son of a late wildlife artist has flown from New Zealand to the UK because he wants his father's work to receive the recognition he believes it deserves.

Peter Partington, who lived in Kettlebaston, Suffolk, created hundreds of pieces of art dedicated to nature before his death in March 2025.

His son, Jerome Partington, has now created a book to honour Peter's life's work and is hosting events in aid of charities that were close to his father's heart.

Jerome said: "When Dad died a bit out of the blue. I thought thousands of people knew him, but he hadn't had much recognition. So we created this book, and in a way, Dad's done all the hard work. He's painted all these incredible pictures...I've just put them together in a way that hopefully tells a story."

Jerome, who is now based near Auckland in New Zealand, explained his father had always had a love of nature and art from a young age.

He said he had fond memories of his father often showing him insects and flowers while in the garden or enjoying walks together.

His father's love of art and nature also inspired him to pursue his own career in architecture, where he incorporates ecological and regenerative practices.

Partington had his own studio in Lavenham and Jerome said Suffolk had provided much inspiration.

"He would go to each nature reserve in Suffolk and south Norfolk, a few times a year," he continued.

"He knew them all by heart and had all sorts of friends he went there with.

"He loved it, absolutely loved it. He needed no excuse to get out that door with his binoculars and his sketch pad."

Jerome has travelled back to the UK to host events for the book titled The Artists Anthology.

He will be travelling to Sudbury, Lavenham, St Neots in Cambridgeshire and near Gloucester this month.

A share of the sales will go toward creating a bursary for wildlife artists to work with young people and for nature charities.
